name: Indigo naturalis (Qing-Dai)
short: Linked to pulmonary arterial hypertension, persistent in 35% of 20 cases in one study, and to intussusception (40% of 10 cases needed surgery) and liver dysfunction in ulcerative colitis.
text: Qing-Dai has been linked to pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), and a 2025 study notes that the 2022 European cardiology and respiratory society guidelines list it as a drug associated with PAH; in that retrospective multicentre study of 20 patients in Japan diagnosed with PAH after a median of 4.8 years of Qing-Dai use, pressures improved after stopping Qing-Dai and using PAH medicines, but 7 (35%) had persistent PAH despite treatment and one relapsed. A Japanese nationwide questionnaire survey of 877 patients with ulcerative colitis treated with indigo naturalis recorded adverse events in 91, including liver dysfunction (40, tending to be mild and reversible), gastrointestinal symptoms (21), headache (13) and PAH (11, which recovered in patients who stopped), plus 10 cases of intussusception, 40% of which needed surgical resection; no deaths were reported. A systematic review found PAH in 14 of 1,158 patients (1.2%), and a survey of children with ulcerative colitis recorded one case of PAH and five of enteritis. In an 8-week placebo-controlled trial in 86 patients with active ulcerative colitis, mild liver dysfunction occurred in 10 patients given indigo naturalis and no serious adverse events were observed, but the trial was stopped after a report of PAH in a patient who had used self-purchased indigo naturalis for 6 months, and the authors concluded it should not yet be used because of the potential for adverse effects including PAH. In contrast, a 2-week placebo-controlled trial of capsules in 42 patients reported no serious adverse events such as pulmonary hypertension or intussusception, with mild headache in 5 patients given indigo naturalis and 1 given placebo. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
